claim: Mitochondrial dysfunction is a hallmark of aging.
source: Mitochondrial dysfunction is a hallmark of aging, and underlies the development of many diseases.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by established scientific consensus in the field of aging research.

claim: Mitochondrial dysfunction underlies the development of many diseases.
source: Mitochondrial dysfunction is a hallmark of aging, and underlies the development of many diseases.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by established scientific consensus.

claim: A new mitochondrial degradation system remodels the mitochondrial proteome of aged yeast cells.
source: Here, using yeast as a model system, we identify a new mitochondrial degradation system that remodels the mitochondrial proteome of aged cells.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The MDC system selectively removes a subset of membrane proteins from the mitochondrial inner and outer membranes while leaving the remainder of the organelle intact.
source: Unlike many common mitochondrial degradation pathways, this system selectively removes a subset of membrane proteins from the mitochondrial inner and outer membranes, while leaving the remainder of the organelle intact.
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data showing selective protein incorporation into MDCs (Figure 5) and exclusion of other mitochondrial proteins.

claim: Selective removal of preexisting proteins is achieved by sorting into a mitochondrial-derived compartment (MDC), followed by release through mitochondrial fission and elimination by autophagy.
source: Selective removal of preexisting proteins is achieved by sorting into a mitochondrial-derived compartment, or MDC, followed by release through mitochondrial fission and elimination by autophagy.
evidence: This is supported by data showing MDC formation (Figure 4), requirement for fission machinery (Figure 1A, Figure 4C), and autophagy dependence (Figure 1A, Figure 2C-D).

claim: Formation of MDCs requires the import receptors Tom70/71.
source: Formation of MDCs requires the import receptors Tom70/71, and failure to form these structures exacerbates preexisting mitochondrial dysfunction, suggesting that the MDC pathway provides protection to mitochondria in times of stress.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 7B-C showing that deletion of TOM70 and TOM71 prevents MDC formation.

claim: Failure to form MDCs exacerbates preexisting mitochondrial dysfunction.
source: Formation of MDCs requires the import receptors Tom70/71, and failure to form these structures exacerbates preexisting mitochondrial dysfunction, suggesting that the MDC pathway provides protection to mitochondria in times of stress.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 7D showing greater loss of membrane potential in tom70Δ and tom70Δ tom71Δ cells treated with concanamycin A.

claim: The MDC pathway provides protection to mitochondria in times of stress.
source: Formation of MDCs requires the import receptors Tom70/71, and failure to form these structures exacerbates preexisting mitochondrial dysfunction, suggesting that the MDC pathway provides protection to mitochondria in times of stress.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that cells lacking Tom70/71 show greater mitochondrial dysfunction when stressed.

claim: Mitochondria play a central role in cellular metabolism.
source: Mitochondria play a central role in cellular metabolism.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about mitochondrial function.

claim: Metabolic pathways that occur within mitochondria include the TCA cycle, oxidative phosphorylation, amino acid metabolism, and biosynthesis of lipids, heme, and iron-sulfur clusters.
source: Metabolic pathways that occur within mitochondria include the TCA cycle, oxidative phosphorylation, amino acid metabolism, and biosynthesis of lipids, heme, and iron-sulfur clusters (Rutter and Hughes, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Cells have evolved multiple mechanisms to maintain mitochondrial homeostasis under diverse physiological states.
source: Because so many vital processes take place within mitochondria, cells have evolved multiple mechanisms to maintain mitochondrial homeostasis under the diverse array of physiological states that a cell can exist in.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about cellular adaptation mechanisms.

claim: Failure to maintain mitochondrial homeostasis contributes to the development of numerous age-associated and metabolic disorders.
source: Failure to maintain mitochondrial homeostasis under these conditions contributes to the development of numerous age-associated and metabolic disorders (Nunnari and Suomalainen, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Mitochondrial adaptive responses are manifested through the composition and activity of approximately 1000 mitochondrial proteins.
source: Many of the adaptive responses made by mitochondria are manifested through the composition and activity of the ~1000 mitochondrial proteins, which are regulated at multiple points from transcription to degradation (Bohovych et al., 2015; Fox, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Cells are equipped with numerous proteolytic pathways that function to maintain mitochondrial homeostasis.
source: In the area of mitochondrial protein degradation, cells are equipped with numerous proteolytic pathways that function to maintain mitochondrial homeostasis (Anand et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Some mitochondrial degradation pathways target individual mitochondrial proteins, whereas others act more broadly and remove large portions of the organelle.
source: Some of these pathways target individual mitochondrial proteins, whereas others act more broadly and remove large portions of the organelle.
evidence: This is established knowledge about different types of mitochondrial quality control pathways.

claim: AAA+-ATPase proteases within all mitochondrial compartments promote the degradation of unassembled protein complex subunits, oxidatively damaged proteins, and tail-anchored membrane proteins mistargeted to the mitochondrial outer membrane.
source: Examples of the former include AAA+-ATPase proteases within all mitochondrial compartments that promote the degradation of unassembled protein complex subunits, oxidatively damaged proteins, and tail-anchored membrane proteins mistargeted to the mitochondrial outer membrane (Chen et al., 2014; Gerdes et al., 2012; Okreglak and Walter, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to primary research articles.

claim: There are proteasome-dependent pathways that promote the turnover of proteins in the mitochondrial outer membrane and within internal mitochondrial compartments.
source: There are also proteasome-dependent pathways that promote the turnover of proteins in the mitochondrial outer membrane and within internal mitochondrial compartments (Taylor and Rutter, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: The best-studied pathway for destruction of large portions of mitochondria is through selective autophagy, or mitophagy.
source: The best-studied pathway for destruction of large portions of mitochondria is through selective autophagy, or mitophagy (Youle and Narendra, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: In metazoa, the PINK1/Parkin pathway serves as a paradigm of mitophagy.
source: In metazoa, the PINK1/Parkin pathway serves as a paradigm of mitophagy (Pickrell and Youle, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: PINK1 is a mitochondrial-localized kinase that is rapidly turned over in healthy mitochondria, but becomes stabilized on the surface of mitochondria with a reduced mitochondrial membrane potential.
source: PINK1 is a mitochondrial-localized kinase that is rapidly turned over in healthy mitochondria, but becomes stabilized on the surface of mitochondria with a reduced mitochondrial membrane potential, or △Ψ (Narendra et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a primary research article.

claim: Upon stabilization, PINK1 recruits the E3 ligase Parkin, which ubiquitinates a number of mitochondrial surface proteins to promote fragmentation and destruction of dysfunctional mitochondria in the lysosome by autophagy.
source: Upon stabilization, PINK1 recruits the E3 ligase Parkin, which ubiquitinates a number of mitochondrial surface proteins to promote fragmentation and destruction of dysfunctional mitochondria in the lysosome by autophagy (Narendra et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a primary research article.

claim: All the general machinery of autophagy must be active for mitophagy to occur.
source: Importantly, all the general machinery of autophagy must be active for mitophagy to occur.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the requirements for mitophagy.

claim: The budding yeast S. cerevisiae contains no obvious sequence homologs of PINK1 and Parkin.
source: The budding yeast, S. cerevisiae, contains no obvious sequence homologs of PINK1 and Parkin, but there are multiple reports of mitophagy occurring in yeast when cells are metabolically challenged or when △Ψ is compromised by genetic mutation or chemical treatment (Kanki et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: There are multiple reports of mitophagy occurring in yeast when cells are metabolically challenged or when mitochondrial membrane potential is compromised by genetic mutation or chemical treatment.
source: The budding yeast, S. cerevisiae, contains no obvious sequence homologs of PINK1 and Parkin, but there are multiple reports of mitophagy occurring in yeast when cells are metabolically challenged or when △Ψ is compromised by genetic mutation or chemical treatment (Kanki et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: The most clearly defined version of mitophagy in budding yeast requires a mitochondrial outer membrane protein, Atg32, to link fragments of mitochondria to the autophagy machinery for degradation.
source: The most clearly defined version of mitophagy in budding yeast requires a mitochondrial outer membrane protein, Atg32, to link fragments of mitochondria to the autophagy machinery for degradation (Kanki et al., 2009b; Okamoto et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to primary research articles.

claim: The Atg32 pathway does not appear to respond to loss of mitochondrial membrane potential and does not utilize ubiquitin tagging for mitochondrial destruction.
source: Unlike the PINK1/Parkin pathway, the Atg32 pathway does not appear to respond to loss of △Ψ and does not utilize ubiquitin tagging for mitochondrial destruction.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the differences between PINK1/Parkin and Atg32 pathways.

claim: Expression of Atg32 on the surface of mitochondria promotes turnover of mitochondria, primarily during times of regulated metabolic remodeling such as during the transition from robust growth to a starved or stationary phase-like state.
source: Instead, expression of Atg32 on the surface of mitochondria promotes turnover of mitochondria, primarily during times of regulated metabolic remodeling such as during the transition from robust growth to a starved or stationary phase-like state.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Atg32-dependent mitophagy.

claim: Atg32-dependent mitophagy may be a functional homologue to the tagging of mitochondria by the NIX protein during reticulocyte maturation.
source: In this regard, Atg32-dependent mitophagy may be a functional homologue to the tagging of mitochondria by the NIX protein during reticulocyte maturation (Novak et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative comparison supported by citation to a primary research article.

claim: NIX is proposed to serve as a receptor on mitochondria to mediate mitophagy during reticulocyte maturation.
source: NIX is proposed to serve as a receptor on mitochondria to mediate mitophagy in this developmental process.
evidence: This is established knowledge about NIX function.

claim: A second mode of eliminating large portions of mitochondria was discovered in mammalian cells involving the formation of mitochondrial-derived vesicles (MDVs).
source: More recently, a second mode of eliminating large portions of mitochondria was discovered in mammalian cells. It involves the formation of mitochondrial-derived vesicles (MDVs), which deliver oxidized mitochondrial proteins to the lysosome for degradation (Soubannier et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a primary research article.

claim: MDVs deliver oxidized mitochondrial proteins to the lysosome for degradation.
source: More recently, a second mode of eliminating large portions of mitochondria was discovered in mammalian cells. It involves the formation of mitochondrial-derived vesicles (MDVs), which deliver oxidized mitochondrial proteins to the lysosome for degradation (Soubannier et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a primary research article.

claim: PINK1/Parkin are needed for MDV formation and degradation, but the core autophagy machinery is not required.
source: PINK1/Parkin are also needed for MDV formation and degradation, but interestingly the core autophagy machinery is not required (McLelland et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a primary research article.

claim: MDVs may provide an early wave of mitochondrial protein quality control, which if unsuccessful in re-achieving cellular homeostasis, is followed by 'full blown' mitophagy.
source: This has led to the speculation that MDVs may provide an early wave of mitochondrial protein quality control, which if unsuccessful in re-achieving cellular homeostasis, is followed by 'full blown' mitophagy (Sugiura et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative model supported by citation to a review article.

claim: There has long been a strong association between cellular aging and mitochondrial dysfunction.
source: There has long been a strong association between cellular aging and mitochondrial dysfunction (Gonzalez-Freire et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: There is an incomplete understanding of how mitochondrial degradation systems contribute to promoting mitochondrial health in aging organisms.
source: However, there is an incomplete understanding of how these degradation systems contribute to promoting mitochondrial health in aging organisms.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Mutations in PINK1/Parkin lead to early onset of neurodegeneration.
source: While mutations in PINK1/Parkin lead to early onset of neurodegeneration (Kitada et al., 1998; Valente et al., 2004), it is not yet clear what events trigger this dependence on the PINK1/Parkin pathway during the aging process.
evidence: This is supported by citations to primary research articles.

claim: It is not yet clear what events trigger dependence on the PINK1/Parkin pathway during the aging process.
source: While mutations in PINK1/Parkin lead to early onset of neurodegeneration (Kitada et al., 1998; Valente et al., 2004), it is not yet clear what events trigger this dependence on the PINK1/Parkin pathway during the aging process.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Much of what is known about mitophagy and MDVs is based primarily upon acute stresses placed on mitochondria by chemical challenges or severe genetic perturbations.
source: In fact, much of what is known about mitophagy and MDVs is based primarily upon acute stresses placed on mitochondria by chemical challenges or severe genetic perturbations (e.g. treatments that cause global ROS damage or complete loss of △Ψ) (Sugiura et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Replicative aging of S. cerevisiae functions as a model system for understanding fundamental aspects of cellular aging, including age-dependent mitochondrial dysfunction.
source: Replicative aging of S. cerevisiae, defined by the number of times an individual yeast cell produces a daughter cell, functions as a model system for understanding fundamental aspects of cellular aging, including age-dependent mitochondrial dysfunction (Breitenbach et al., 2014; Steinkraus et al., 2008; Wasko and Kaeberlein, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Aged yeast cells have reduced mitochondrial membrane potential, decreased mitochondrial import, and altered mitochondrial morphology that transitions from a typical tubular shape to one that is highly fragmented and amorphous with increasing age.
source: We and others have shown that aged yeast cells have reduced △Ψ, decreased mitochondrial import, and altered mitochondrial morphology that transitions from a typical tubular shape to one that is highly fragmented and amorphous with increasing age (Hughes and Gottschling, 2012; Lam et al., 2011; McFaline-Figueroa et al., 2011; Scheckhuber et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to primary research articles including the authors' previous work.

claim: Age-associated changes in mitochondrial structure and function are driven at least in part by changes in the pH of the yeast lysosome-like vacuole that occur earlier in the yeast cell's age.
source: This change in mitochondrial structure and function is driven at least in part by changes in the pH of the yeast lysosome-like vacuole that occur earlier in the yeast cell's age (Hughes and Gottschling, 2012), as well as asymmetric partitioning of healthy mitochondria to daughter cells (McFaline-Figueroa et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to primary research articles including the authors' previous work.

claim: Age-associated changes in mitochondrial structure and function are driven in part by asymmetric partitioning of healthy mitochondria to daughter cells.
source: This change in mitochondrial structure and function is driven at least in part by changes in the pH of the yeast lysosome-like vacuole that occur earlier in the yeast cell's age (Hughes and Gottschling, 2012), as well as asymmetric partitioning of healthy mitochondria to daughter cells (McFaline-Figueroa et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a primary research article.

claim: No GFP signal from Tom70-GFP was detected in the vacuole of wild-type cells across a wide range of ages.
source: No GFP signal was detected in the vacuole of wild-type cells across a wide range of ages (data not shown).
evidence: This is an observation from the study, though the data is not shown.

claim: Vacuolar proteases rapidly degrade proteins taken up by autophagy and thus frequently prevent protein detection in the vacuole.
source: However, vacuolar proteases rapidly degrade proteins taken up by autophagy and thus frequently prevent protein detection in the vacuole.
evidence: This is established knowledge about vacuolar protein degradation.

claim: In young cells with functional mitochondria, no Tom70-GFP was detected in vacuoles by fluorescence microscopy.
source: In young cells, which had functional mitochondria, no Tom70-GFP was detected in vacuoles by fluorescence microscopy (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Vacuoles in 70% of aged cells contained Tom70-GFP.
source: However, vacuoles in 70% of aged cells contained Tom70-GFP (marked by white arrows in Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data and quantification shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Tom70-GFP in the vacuole appeared as a body exhibiting constant Brownian motion within the boundary of the vacuole membrane.
source: Tom70-GFP in the vacuole appeared as a body exhibiting constant Brownian motion within the boundary of the vacuole membrane (data not shown), which is characteristic of autophagosomes that cannot be broken down in pep4△ cells (Takeshige et al., 1992).
evidence: This is an observation from the study supported by citation to a primary research article about autophagosome behavior.

claim: Brownian motion within the vacuole boundary is characteristic of autophagosomes that cannot be broken down in pep4Δ cells.
source: Tom70-GFP in the vacuole appeared as a body exhibiting constant Brownian motion within the boundary of the vacuole membrane (data not shown), which is characteristic of autophagosomes that cannot be broken down in pep4△ cells (Takeshige et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a primary research article.

claim: Aged atg5Δ pep4Δ cells contained no Tom70-GFP in the vacuole.
source: Aged atg5△ pep4△ cells contained no Tom70-GFP in the vacuole, which indicated that Tom70-GFP normally entered the vacuole via autophagy (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Tom70-GFP normally enters the vacuole via autophagy.
source: Aged atg5△ pep4△ cells contained no Tom70-GFP in the vacuole, which indicated that Tom70-GFP normally entered the vacuole via autophagy (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that deletion of ATG5 prevents Tom70-GFP vacuolar delivery.

claim: Some forms of mitochondrial autophagy require the mitochondrial fission machinery.
source: In addition to the core autophagy machinery, some forms of mitochondrial autophagy require the mitochondrial fission machinery (Muller et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Delivery of Tom70-GFP to the vacuole in aged cells requires the mitochondrial fission machinery.
source: Delivery of Tom70-GFP to the vacuole in aged cells also required the mitochondrial fission machinery, as this process was inhibited in cells lacking DNM1, which encodes a conserved GTPase required for mitochondrial fission (Figure 1A) (Bleazard et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data in Figure 1A and citation to a primary research article about Dnm1 function.

claim: DNM1 encodes a conserved GTPase required for mitochondrial fission.
source: Delivery of Tom70-GFP to the vacuole in aged cells also required the mitochondrial fission machinery, as this process was inhibited in cells lacking DNM1, which encodes a conserved GTPase required for mitochondrial fission (Figure 1A) (Bleazard et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a primary research article.

claim: Starvation-induced mitophagy in yeast relies on Atg32, a receptor on the mitochondrial surface that links mitochondria to the autophagy machinery for degradation.
source: Lastly, starvation-induced mitophagy in yeast relies on Atg32, a receptor on the mitochondrial surface that links mitochondria to the autophagy machinery for degradation (Kanki et al., 2009b; Okamoto et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to primary research articles.

claim: Tom70 degradation in aged cells is independent of Atg32.
source: However, Tom70 degradation in aged cells is independent of Atg32; aged cells lacking ATG32 delivered Tom70-GFP to the vacuole at the same level as in wild-type cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data and quantification shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The identified autophagy-dependent pathway for degrading Tom70 in mitochondria from aging yeast cells requires mitochondrial fission and is distinct from the previously characterized Atg32-dependent pathway.
source: These results suggest we identified an autophagy-dependent pathway for degrading Tom70 in mitochondria from aging yeast cells that requires mitochondrial fission and is distinct from the previously characterized Atg32-dependent pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing autophagy and fission dependence but Atg32 independence.

claim: The presence of Tom70 in the vacuole peaks in middle-aged cells, and then declines in old cells.
source: While examining the kinetics of Tom70-GFP vacuolar delivery in aged cells, we noticed that the presence of Tom70 in the vacuole peaked in middle-aged cells, and then declined in old cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data and quantification shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The decline in Tom70-GFP vacuolar delivery in old cells coincides with a highly fragmented vacuole.
source: This decline coincided with a highly fragmented vacuole, depicted in the third panel of Figure 1A.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Vacuoles increase in size with age and then can become severely fragmented in very old cells.
source: For reasons that are unclear, vacuoles increase in size with age and then can become severely fragmented in very old cells (Figure 1A) (Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data in Figure 1A and citation to a primary research article.

claim: In all cells with a severely fragmented vacuole, Tom70-GFP appears in small vesicle-like structures in the cytoplasm.
source: Interestingly, in all cells with a severely fragmented vacuole, Tom70-GFP appears in small vesicle-like structures in the cytoplasm (Figure 1A and Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1A and Video 1.

claim: The small vesicle-like structures containing Tom70-GFP in old cells are not cytosolically-localized autophagosomes.
source: These structures are not cytosolically-localized autophagosomes, because they are still present in old cells lacking ATG5 (Figure 1B and Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data showing persistence of these structures in atg5Δ cells (Figure 1B and Video 2).

claim: Formation of the small vesicle-like structures in old cells requires the mitochondrial fission GTPase DNM1.
source: However, their formation does require the mitochondrial fission GTPase DNM1 (Figure 1B and Video 3).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data showing absence of these structures in dnm1Δ cells (Figure 1B and Video 3).

claim: Mitochondrial protein destruction is activated in middle-aged cells.
source: Thus, although mitochondrial protein destruction is activated in middle-aged cells, this autophagy-dependent degradation appears compromised in very old yeast, leading to production of Dnm1-dependent vesicle-like structures.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Tom70-GFP vacuolar delivery peaks in middle-aged cells.

claim: Autophagy-dependent degradation of mitochondrial proteins appears compromised in very old yeast, leading to production of Dnm1-dependent vesicle-like structures.
source: Thus, although mitochondrial protein destruction is activated in middle-aged cells, this autophagy-dependent degradation appears compromised in very old yeast, leading to production of Dnm1-dependent vesicle-like structures.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Tom70-GFP vacuolar delivery declines in old cells and vesicle-like structures accumulate.

claim: Mitochondrial dysfunction in aged cells is caused by disruption of a metabolic relationship between mitochondria and vacuoles.
source: We previously showed that mitochondrial dysfunction in aged cells is caused by disruption of a metabolic relationship between mitochondria and vacuoles (Hughes and Gottschling, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Vacuoles are acidified by the Vacuolar-H+-ATPase (V-ATPase).
source: Vacuoles are acidified by the Vacuolar-H+-ATPase (V-ATPase) (Kane, 2006), and the proton gradient generated by this protein complex is required for amino acid storage within the vacuole lumen (Klionsky et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review and primary research articles.

claim: The proton gradient generated by the V-ATPase is required for amino acid storage within the vacuole lumen.
source: Vacuoles are acidified by the Vacuolar-H+-ATPase (V-ATPase) (Kane, 2006), and the proton gradient generated by this protein complex is required for amino acid storage within the vacuole lumen (Klionsky et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a primary research article.

claim: Loss of vacuole acidity in aged cells causes mitochondrial dysfunction through an undefined mechanism that likely involves altered storage of cellular amino acids.
source: Loss of vacuole acidity in aged cells causes mitochondrial dysfunction through an undefined mechanism that likely involves altered storage of cellular amino acids (Hughes and Gottschling, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work and involves speculation about the mechanism.

claim: Treatment of young cells with concanamycin A recapitulates age-associated changes in mitochondria.
source: To test if loss of vacuole acidity triggers autophagy-dependent mitochondrial protein degradation, we took advantage of the fact that treatment of young cells with concanamycin A (conc A), a specific inhibitor of the V-ATPase (Drose et al., 1993), recapitulates age-associated changes in mitochondria (Figure 2A) (Hughes and Gottschling, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work and a citation about concanamycin A.

claim: Concanamycin A is a specific inhibitor of the V-ATPase.
source: To test if loss of vacuole acidity triggers autophagy-dependent mitochondrial protein degradation, we took advantage of the fact that treatment of young cells with concanamycin A (conc A), a specific inhibitor of the V-ATPase (Drose et al., 1993), recapitulates age-associated changes in mitochondria (Figure 2A) (Hughes and Gottschling, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a primary research article.

claim: Treatment with concanamycin A causes an immediate loss of vacuolar acidity, followed by a decline in mitochondrial membrane potential within 30 min.
source: Consistent with our previous findings, treatment with conc A caused an immediate loss of vacuolar acidity, followed by a decline in mitochondrial △Ψ within 30 min as measured by microscopy (Figure 2B) using the common mitochondrial membrane potential fluorescent dye DiOC6 (Pringle et al., 1989), or by flow cytometry (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) using DiOC6 and another mitochondrial membrane potential dye, TMRM (Scaduto and Grotyohann, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy and flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, and citations about the dyes used.

claim: DiOC6 is a common mitochondrial membrane potential fluorescent dye.
source: Consistent with our previous findings, treatment with conc A caused an immediate loss of vacuolar acidity, followed by a decline in mitochondrial △Ψ within 30 min as measured by microscopy (Figure 2B) using the common mitochondrial membrane potential fluorescent dye DiOC6 (Pringle et al., 1989), or by flow cytometry (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) using DiOC6 and another mitochondrial membrane potential dye, TMRM (Scaduto and Grotyohann, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a primary research article.

claim: TMRM is a mitochondrial membrane potential dye.
source: Consistent with our previous findings, treatment with conc A caused an immediate loss of vacuolar acidity, followed by a decline in mitochondrial △Ψ within 30 min as measured by microscopy (Figure 2B) using the common mitochondrial membrane potential fluorescent dye DiOC6 (Pringle et al., 1989), or by flow cytometry (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) using DiOC6 and another mitochondrial membrane potential dye, TMRM (Scaduto and Grotyohann, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a primary research article.

claim: Treatment of young cells with concanamycin A causes accumulation of Tom70-GFP-containing bodies within the vacuole.
source: Similar to our observations in aged cells, treatment of young cells with conc A caused accumulation of Tom70-GFP-containing bodies within the vacuole (Figure 2C, white arrows).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Loss of vacuolar acidity triggers activation of the Tom70-GFP degradation pathway.
source: Because no Tom70-GFP was present in the vacuoles of untreated pep4△ cells, we conclude that loss of vacuolar acidity triggers activation of this pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Tom70-GFP appears in vacuoles only after concanamycin A treatment.

claim: In concanamycin A treated cells, it is not necessary to delete PEP4 to observe Tom70-GFP within the vacuole.
source: Additionally, in contrast to old cells, it was not necessary to delete PEP4 to observe Tom70-GFP within the vacuole of conc A treated cells.
evidence: This is an observation from the study.

claim: Inhibition of the V-ATPase with concanamycin A creates an environment within the vacuole lumen that prevents autophagosome breakdown.
source: This is likely because inhibition of the V-ATPase with conc A creates an environment within the lumen that prevents autophagosome breakdown (Nakamura et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a primary research article.

claim: The appearance of Tom70-GFP in the concanamycin A treated vacuole occurs within three hours after mitochondrial depolarization.
source: The appearance of Tom70-GFP in the conc A treated vacuole occurred within three hours after mitochondrial depolarization, and was preceded by the formation of a single bright focus that contained Tom70-GFP, but appeared somewhat distinct from the rest of the mitochondria (Figure 2C, white *).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The appearance of Tom70-GFP in the vacuole is preceded by the formation of a single bright focus that contains Tom70-GFP, but appears somewhat distinct from the rest of the mitochondria.
source: The appearance of Tom70-GFP in the conc A treated vacuole occurred within three hours after mitochondrial depolarization, and was preceded by the formation of a single bright focus that contained Tom70-GFP, but appeared somewhat distinct from the rest of the mitochondria (Figure 2C, white *).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In concanamycin A treated cells, delivery of Tom70-GFP to the vacuole is dependent on both the autophagy (Atg5) and mitochondrial fission machineries (Dnm1), but independent of Atg32.
source: As in old cells, delivery of Tom70-GFP to the vacuole was dependent on both the autophagy (Atg5) and mitochondrial fission machineries (Dnm1), but independent of Atg32 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data and quantification shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Delivery of Tom70-GFP to the vacuole requires the vacuole homotypic fusion protein Vam3, which is essential for fusion of autophagosomes with the vacuole.
source: Further supporting the role of autophagy in this process, delivery of Tom70-GFP to the vacuole also required the vacuole homotypic fusion protein Vam3, which is essential for fusion of autophagosomes with the vacuole (Figure 2C) (Darsow et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data in Figure 2C and citation to a primary research article about Vam3 function.

claim: Vam3 is essential for fusion of autophagosomes with the vacuole.
source: Further supporting the role of autophagy in this process, delivery of Tom70-GFP to the vacuole also required the vacuole homotypic fusion protein Vam3, which is essential for fusion of autophagosomes with the vacuole (Figure 2C) (Darsow et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a primary research article.

claim: Treatment of cells for six hours with concanamycin A causes release of GFP from full length Tom70-GFP.
source: Treatment of cells for six hours caused release of GFP from full length Tom70-GFP (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: GFP cleavage from Tom70-GFP requires the vacuolar protease PEP4, the autophagy and mitochondrial fission machineries, and is independent of ATG32.
source: GFP cleavage required the vacuolar protease PEP4, the autophagy and mitochondrial fission machineries, and was independent of ATG32 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Disruption of the mitochondrial-vacuole relationship by direct V-ATPase inhibition activates autophagy-dependent mitochondrial protein degradation.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that disruption of the mitochondrial-vacuole relationship by direct V-ATPase inhibition activates autophagy-dependent mitochondrial protein degradation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing that concanamycin A treatment triggers Tom70-GFP degradation.

claim: Treatment of cells with antimycin A causes mitochondrial depolarization equal to or greater than concanamycin A.
source: Although treatment of cells with these inhibitors caused mitochondrial depolarization equal to or greater than conc A (Figure 3A and B), we did not observe Tom70-GFP delivery to the vacuole at any point during treatment with these compounds (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Treatment of cells with FCCP causes mitochondrial depolarization equal to or greater than concanamycin A.
source: Although treatment of cells with these inhibitors caused mitochondrial depolarization equal to or greater than conc A (Figure 3A and B), we did not observe Tom70-GFP delivery to the vacuole at any point during treatment with these compounds (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A and B.
